events.text: Day 1 begins.

Day 1 — we're flying blind, so let's set a good precedent: keep an eye on how people argue rather than just what they claim. Early tells matter more than early claims. Watch who pushes hard against someone with no real reason, and watch who conveniently stays quiet when heat lands on them. I don't have any accusations yet — anyone who claims certainty on day 1 is bluffing for attention or trying to look proactive. I'll be listening for genuine reasoning over performance.

Isha here, villager. I agree with Leo that early behavior is more useful than early claims, and I have no accusations yet. Day 1 gives us very little to go on, so I'm treating everyone as unknown. Leo, you said we should watch who conveniently goes quiet when heat lands on them. Does that mean we should weigh silence on Day 1 at all, or only after someone has been pressured?

Good question, Isha. To clarify: I'd weight silence after someone has been pressed — on Day 1 nobody has really been singled out yet, so there's not much pressure to respond to. But going forward, if a player gets called out and the response is evasion rather than a real defense, that's a meaningful tell. It's not about total silence on Day 1 — it's about the pattern once scrutiny lands on someone specifically. Isha, you said you're treating everyone as unknown today — does that mean you'd be equally comfortable voting for anyone based on tomorrow's discussion, or are you hoping to find someone to clear early?

Leo, fair question. I'm not committed to anyone yet, and I'm not trying to clear anyone early. I also won't vote based on first impressions alone. I'd want a concrete reason I can explain, such as a contradiction or an evasive answer to a specific point. Your distinction between Day 1 silence and evasion after pressure is sensible, so I'll apply the same test to everyone, including you.

Two points where I'd push back slightly on the frame that's forming, then my own position.

First, on Leo's "watch who conveniently goes quiet when heat lands on them": as a heuristic that risks manufacturing a false tell. If the group starts treating quietness as suspicious, then the least confident players get punished for lacking nerve, not for being mafia. People under-reasoning and people hiding are not the same thing. I'd rather anchor on Isha's version — concrete contradictions, or an evasive answer to a specific, answerable point — because that measures what someone did, not how they behave under a spotlight nobody deserves yet.

Second, on mechanics: we're nine alive, two mafia, and a leader needs half the living players to be eliminated. Day 1 random votes are close to worthless and cost us a whole cycle while giving mafia a cheap night kill. So I'd rather see today end with a small amount of shared structure — who each of us is least able to vouch for and why — than with a coin-flip. If nobody has a reason, abstention or a near-random vote is at least honest, and it preserves the detective and doctor for actual checks.

My own position: no accusation. I don't have a contradiction to point at, and I won't invent one to look proactive. What I can offer is a commitment — I won't vote for anyone today whose only case against them is that they were quiet or vague; if I do end up voting someone, I'll name the specific thing they said or failed to say that made it my best read. Judge me on that at the vote.

Felix here. I want to build on what Sam laid out, because I think the structure point is the right one for today. We're nine alive with two mafia among us — every vote we cast today is a shot in the dark, and the cost of a bad shot isn't just a wasted day, it's that we lose a cycle while the mafia get a free night kill regardless. So the honest move today is to resist the pressure to manufacture suspicion just to look engaged.

That said, I don't think 'no accusations' has to mean 'no work.' There are a couple of things we can legitimately do today without inventing tells. First, agree on what will count as evidence going forward. Isha's version — a contradiction, or an evasion on a specific answerable point — is a good baseline, and I'd add one more: how someone's story changes under pressure. Not whether they're quiet, but whether what they say on day 2 is compatible with what they said today. That's why it matters that we're all putting our positions on the record now, even non-committal ones. People who've committed to a framework today are harder to quietly walk away from tomorrow.

Second, we should be careful about the voting mechanics tomorrow. Sam is right that a leader needs half the living players, which is five votes out of nine today. That's a high bar, which means the realistic outcomes are either a broad consensus target or nobody. I'd rather we end today with nobody eliminated than burn a villager on vibes — but I also don't want 'abstain by default' to become a shield people hide behind on day 2 and day 3, when we'll actually have information from the night. So my proposal: today, no vote unless someone can articulate a specific reason, and the burden is on the accuser, not the accused. Tomorrow, that changes — if you abstain after a night kill gives us data, you should have to explain what you're waiting for.

On my own position: no accusation, same as everyone else so far, and for the same reason — I don't have a contradiction to point at, and I won't fake one. What I can commit to is this: I'll vote only where I can name the specific statement or non-response that changed my read, and I'll hold everyone else to that same standard, including people who are being loud and confident about their process. Honestly, the people performing reasonableness the hardest on day 1 can be just as suspicious as the people going quiet — the tell isn't volume either way, it's whether the reasoning survives contact with specifics. I plan to hold everyone's stated positions against what they say after tonight, and I'd encourage the rest of you to do the same with mine.

Felix, I'll take that last point directly — you're right that confidence in process can itself be a performance, and I'll own that my opening was exactly the kind of thing you're warning about: a lot of "watch how people argue" framing that can read as safe positioning. The difference I'd defend is that at least it's on the record — I've said clearly what I'd consider a real tell (evasion after targeted pressure, not just quietness), and I'll be held to that tomorrow.

On structure, I'm aligned with both Felix and Sam: no manufactured accusation today, and no vote unless someone names a specific statement or non-response. But I want to push one practical point — Felix said the burden is on the accuser, not the accused. I agree for today, but tomorrow when we have a night kill to work with, that asymmetry gets dangerous. If the town has a confirmed suspect and the accused just says "prove it," the burden shouldn't stay entirely on the accuser. At some point, being unable to explain yourself under direct questioning becomes its own data point — not a conviction, but a legitimate reason to shift a read. I'd rather we all agree on that now than relitigate it when the stakes are higher.

My commitment stands: I won't vote for anyone whose only case against them is tone or volume, and I expect the same standard applied to me after tonight.

Leo, thanks for taking my point head-on — and I actually agree with the distinction you're drawing about tomorrow. The burden shouldn't stay one-sided forever. Once we have a night kill, an accused player who can't or won't respond to direct, answerable questions is giving us information, and I'm happy to put that on the record now: after tonight, if someone is named for a specific reason and answers with pure deflection, that counts toward my read on them. It's not a conviction standard, but it's data. On your concern about my opening being performance: fair hit. All I'd say is that the difference between safe positioning and useful process is whether the framework actually gets used. I've committed to a concrete test — vote only where I can name the statement or non-response that changed my read. Hold me to that after tonight. If I come back tomorrow voting on vibes, you'll all have earned the right to call that out. Where I want to push the group now: five of us have spoken, and we've largely converged on a shared standard — no manufactured accusations today, evidence means a contradiction or an evasion on a specific answerable point, and Isha's framework seems to be the working baseline. That's genuinely good structure for a day one. But convergence among five people isn't the same as a group position, and there are four players who haven't weighed in yet. Sam made a point I want to echo: what each of us is least able to vouch for, and why, is more useful than a coin-flip vote. That question is still open for most of the table. I'd also flag one thing for whoever speaks next: Sam committed to never voting for someone whose only case against them is quietness or vagueness, and I've made a similar commitment. Leo has too. That's three of us with stated, falsifiable positions on the record. I'd like to hear the same from the rest of the room — not because silence today is suspicious, but because committing now is what makes our day-two behavior legible. If you won't commit to a standard, that's allowed, but say so plainly rather than leaving it ambiguous, because tomorrow we'll be judging each other against what was said today. To be clear about my own state: no accusation, no suspect, no read I'd act on. I'm not going to invent one just because the conversation is warm and it would look proactive. The most useful thing I can do today is help lock in the standard and put my position where it can be checked later. Priya — you've been quiet so far, and I'm not reading anything into that. But since you haven't spoken, I'd genuinely like your answer to the question Sam posed and hasn't been answered by most of the table: is there anything said today that you'd flag as even slightly off, or do you also have no read? Either answer helps us —

Felix, to answer your question directly: I don't have a concrete scum read yet either, and I won't manufacture one just to appear proactive.

If there is anything I'd flag as slightly concerning, it's not a specific contradiction, but rather how comfortable this loop has become. Leo, Sam, and you have spent several turns refining the meta-rules of engagement. Agreeing on sensible standards—like not lynching on vibes or quietness when five votes are needed—is good town hygiene. However, deep procedural discussion is also exceptionally safe territory. Mafia players often thrive in meta-conversations because they can generate town credit and cooperative rapport without taking any real risks or committing to stances on individuals.

I share the baseline that a blind Day 1 elimination risks handing mafia a free tempo advantage, and I commit to not voting unless someone exhibits an actual contradiction or clear evasion. That said, four players—Noah, Lucia, Zara, and Theo—haven't weighed in at all yet. Before we over-polish the framework, we need to hear where the rest of the table stands.

Noah here. I’m arriving late to the discussion, so I’ll be direct: I have no suspect and I won’t invent one. I agree with the working baseline — no Day 1 vote unless someone can name a specific contradiction or an evasion on an answerable point. I also agree with Priya that the amount of procedural agreement is itself worth watching. A shared standard is useful, but it can become a comfortable place for mafia to sound cooperative without taking any real risk on individuals.

My own commitment: today I’ll judge people by whether their stated standard survives specifics, not by volume or confidence. Tomorrow, after a night result, I won’t treat “no read yet” as automatically acceptable if there’s a concrete question someone is dodging. That cuts both ways — I expect to be held to the same test.

Theo, you’re one of the players who hasn’t spoken yet, and Priya raised a specific concern: that deep procedural discussion can be safe territory for mafia because it builds rapport without committing on individuals. Do you agree with that concern, and if so, what non-procedural commitment will you make for Day 2 — meaning what kind of concrete evidence would actually move your read? If you have no read today, say that plainly.

Noah, I agree that procedural agreement is safe territory for mafia, but it isn't evidence against any particular person. I have no scum read today.

Tomorrow, a specific contradiction or an evasion of a direct question would move my read, as would a vote that doesn't match the voter's stated reasoning. I'll look at the revealed votes as well as the night result, and I won't assume a night kill necessarily gives us a clear suspect. I also don't think a contradiction is the only possible reason to vote: a consistent pattern of selectively applying standards could matter, provided I can explain it with examples.

One correction to the discussion: abstaining doesn't preserve everyone through the night; mafia still get an attack, though the doctor might prevent a death. A mistaken elimination costs us another player, so neither option is free.

Zara here. I’ve read the thread. No suspect, and no manufactured accusation. I agree with the working standard: on Day 1, vote only if someone names a specific contradiction or an evasion on an answerable point; otherwise abstain. I also agree with Priya and Noah that procedural agreement is safe territory and shouldn’t earn town credit by itself — but I won’t treat it as evidence against anyone either. My commitment: tomorrow I’ll judge stated standards against specifics, including my own. If someone is asked a concrete, answerable question and deflects, that shifts my read; if I vote, I’ll name the exact statement or non-response that moved me. I’m not yielding this turn; no question from me is needed to keep discussion moving. I have no read I’d act on today.

Lucia here, villager. Since I'm the last one checking in today, I'll keep this grounded. I agree with the broad consensus: with nine alive and five votes required to eliminate, casting speculative votes on Day 1 without concrete evidence risks a mislynch and hands mafia an easy tempo advantage. Unless someone presents an actual contradiction or evades a direct, answerable question before the vote, abstaining today makes the most tactical sense.

I also share the caution raised by Priya, Noah, and Zara about meta-procedural discussion. Agreeing on standards is sensible town hygiene, but it's also very safe ground where mafia can easily look cooperative without taking stances. Today that was somewhat inevitable because we started with zero information, but that grace period ends with the first night phase. Tomorrow we'll have night results and voting records to analyze, and that's when process talk stops being enough.

My commitment matches what several of you have put on the record: I will not vote on vibes, tone, or mere quietness. I'll judge players by whether their actions and reads stay consistent with what they committed to today, and whether they can defend their stances when questioned. I have no accusations today, and I'm not yielding.

All nine of us have spoken, and the useful thing to say is that the table has actually converged on something checkable. Six players have now put a falsifiable standard on the record — no vote without a named contradiction or a named evasion on an answerable point, and an explicit promise to judge people by whether their stated standard survives specifics. That's a real artifact, and it's more than most Day 1s produce.

Three things I want to add, then one question for Theo.

First, a correction I endorse: Theo's right that abstaining doesn't freeze the board — mafia still get an attack, and a wrong elimination still costs us a player. So "abstain because the bar is high" isn't free. It just means we're trading a guaranteed bad elimination for a likely night death. I'll accept that tradeoff today, but everyone should accept that on Day 2 the same logic has to be re-argued from scratch, not inherited.

Second, I want to name the thing we should avoid tomorrow. Priya's point stands and I'll sharpen it: a table that spends Day 2 refining meta-rules has wasted the one day it had real information. So my proposal is concrete — tomorrow, after the night result, every player states one specific claim about one named player before anyone asks for a vote. Not an accusation, a claim: something you believe about how that person behaves or argued. If you can't name a specific claim about a specific person, you have no vote, and you should say so plainly.

Third, the clause I want pinned down. Theo, you said a contradiction isn't the only possible reason to vote — that "a consistent pattern of selectively applying standards could matter." I think that's the right instinct and the least falsifiable statement on the table, because "pattern" and "selectively" can be asserted about anyone after the fact. So, concretely: what would move your read tomorrow beyond a contradiction, and what would move it away again? If your answer is a criterion you could apply identically to any player without reference to who they are, then it isn't a standard yet — it's a license. That's my question, and it's the only one I'm asking.

My own position hasn't changed: no read, no vote today. On Day 2 I will name the specific statement or non-response that moved me, and I expect anyone voting to do the same.

Sam, here's an example: if someone calls one player's specific unanswered question suspicious but excuses another player's comparable evasion without explaining the difference, that would move my read against them. I'd cite both exchanges and ask what distinction they see. A convincing difference in context, or a correction showing I misread an answer, would move my read back.

That standard applies to anyone, including me. I wouldn't treat one inconsistent judgment as proof of mafia; I'd look at the explanation and any repeated examples. And to clarify the tradeoff: a Day 1 elimination without a strong case isn't guaranteed to be wrong, though it carries a real risk of eliminating town. I still have no read I'd vote on today.

Closing Day 1 with my third and final turn, so let me put everything on the record in a form you can check tomorrow.

My position: no read, no accusation, and I won't vote today. Leo, Felix, Isha, Noah, Zara, Theo, Lucia, Priya — we're converged, and the convergence is real, but it's convergence on procedure, not on anyone in this room. If we lynch a villager tonight on nothing, we hand mafia tempo and we hand the next night to them. A wrong elimination costs a player; abstention doesn't cost a player but it does let mafia kill. Those aren't equivalent, and Theo's correction was the right one to make.

One thing I want to add, because I think the table has missed it and it changes tomorrow's calculus. Theo said abstaining isn't free because mafia still get an attack. That's true for one night. But the win condition is count-based, and nobody has said this out loud: a table that keeps choosing to abstain can never reduce mafia's number, and mafia never reduce ours on their own beyond the night kill. Perpetual abstention is a mafia-favored trajectory. Day 1 abstention is defensible precisely because we have zero information and a bad shot burns a villager. Day 2 abstention with a night result on the table is a different decision, and if we make it by default rather than by argument, we've drifted into the exact safe loop Priya named.

So my Day 2 commitments, stated now so they're falsifiable:

1. I will not vote for anyone whose only case is tone, volume, or quietness.
2. I will vote for someone only if I can name the exact statement or non-response that moved my read, and I'll name it out loud at the vote.
3. If I abstain on Day 2, I will say what I'm waiting for, and it will not be "more process."
4. If I fail any of those three, call me on it in the open — don't let me launder a vibe through a nice-sounding framework.

I'll also say plainly what I haven't done: I haven't named a specific claim about a specific player, which is what I asked everyone for tomorrow. I don't have one. I won't manufacture one on Day 1 and pretend it's a lead.

Priya — you've been the sharpest voice on the risk in this room, and you raised it early and alone. One question, and it's the only one I'm asking: if abstention is not merely neutral but leans mafia over time, does your commitment to not vote without a concrete contradiction still hold as your default on Day 2, or does it change once there's a night result and a record to weigh? If your answer is that you'd still default to abstention, I want to know that now, because that's the position most likely to cost us the game. Isha — nothing for you; I'd rather not spend a question I don't have.

Sam, to answer your question directly: no, abstention will not be my default on Day 2.

The rationale for abstaining today rests entirely on Day 1's unique information void—nine players, zero hard data, and a five-vote threshold where a speculative push carries a high probability of mislynching town. But perpetual abstention is indeed a mafia win condition. With each unresolved cycle, town bleeds numbers while mafia avoid having to defend themselves or their voting behavior under pressure.

Tomorrow the game changes. We will have the night result, the recorded Day 1 votes, and a baseline of what everyone committed to today. On Day 2, waiting exclusively for an explicit, undeniable contradiction before casting a vote is too passive; competent mafia rarely make obvious factual slips. My threshold tomorrow broadens to include voting anomalies, shifts in positioning relative to today's commitments, and how players respond when targeted with legitimate questions.

Abstaining on Day 1 is tactical caution; defaulting to abstention on Day 2 is surrender. Once we have new information on the table tomorrow, I expect active, non-procedural stances from everyone, myself included.

Isha here. I've read the thread and I'm holding my position: no accusation and no vote today. I agree with Sam that abstaining can't become the default on Day 2 once we have a night result. Abstaining on Day 1 is a reasonable response to zero information, but repeating it without argument favors mafia over every cycle. Whatever standard we set, we should apply it to people's actual votes and statements tomorrow, not to who they are. Theo, you haven't answered Sam's question yet. Sam asked what would move your read beyond a contradiction, and you said a pattern of selectively applied standards could matter. Can you give one concrete example of what you would count as selective application, and what explanation would show it was justified?

Isha, I did answer Sam in e16: if someone calls one player's unanswered question suspicious but excuses a comparable evasion by another player without explaining the difference, that would move my read against them. I'd cite both exchanges and ask for their reasoning. A relevant difference in context, or a correction showing I misread an answer, would move my read back.

I still have no read I'd vote on today. Tomorrow I won't require an obvious contradiction: inconsistent application of standards, votes that don't match stated reasoning, and responses to specific questions can all be relevant. I'll explain any vote or abstention, and I won't assume the night result alone points to a suspect.
Voting begins.
The votes are revealed.
All players abstained. Nobody is eliminated.
Night begins.
Mafia target preferences are shared privately before the final kill vote.
Sam is not mafia.
Sam was eliminated.
Day 2 begins.

Sam's death is the first real datum, and I don't want to waste it by relitigating Day 1 process. Sam was the player most explicitly warning that default abstention favors mafia, and he was killed before Day 2 could test that. That doesn't clear or condemn anyone by itself; a kill can be strategic or framing. What I want today is one concrete Day 1 statement each of us would now treat as evidence, not a promise to look for evidence later. My own: I have no scum read yet, and I won't pretend the night kill gives me one. But I will not support another default abstention unless someone names what they are waiting for and why that wait is worth another night. Felix, you committed to naming the exact statement or non-response that changed your read. Now that Sam is dead and we have no vote record, what specific Day 1 statement or non-response is closest to moving your read, and why? If the honest answer is none, say that and say what Day 2 event would move it.

Noah, I'll answer you directly, because I promised I would and because the question is fair.

Honest answer: no specific Day 1 statement or non-response has moved my read yet. Everyone who spoke put a consistent position on the record, nobody contradicted themselves, and the vote record is empty — all nine of us abstained, so there are no vote-versus-reasoning anomalies to examine. I'm not going to retroactively manufacture a suspect out of Day 1 conversation just because the night gave us a body. That would be exactly the vibe-voting I said I wouldn't do.

But I do want to say what the night result does tell us, because I think it's more than nothing. Sam was the player who named the abstention trap most explicitly — he said out loud that default abstention is a mafia-favored trajectory, and he committed to naming a claim about a named player today. He was killed the same night. That's not evidence against anyone by itself; the obvious reading is simply that mafia removed the loudest voice pushing for active voting. But it does sharpen what I said yesterday: the incentive structure right now favors people who keep this table in the 'no read, wait another cycle' loop. Every additional voteless day costs us a player and costs the mafia nothing. So I'm watching for exactly one thing today: who argues for another default abstention now that we have a night result and a written record, and whether their argument acknowledges the cost Sam died highlighting. Theo, Lucia, Zara, Isha, Priya — you all endorsed versions of the abstention standard on Day 1. That was correct then. Today I need to hear from each of you what changed and what you're waiting for, or what you're acting on. That's not an accusation; it's the standard we all agreed to apply.

What would move my read concretely, so you can check me on it: first, anyone who pushes to repeat Day 1's abstention without engaging Sam's argument or offering what they're waiting for. Second, a stated standard today that's visibly weaker than the one the same player stated yesterday — I have all of our commitments on record and I'll be comparing. Third, an answer to a direct question that deflects onto process rather than engaging the specific point asked.

And to keep my own account clean: if by the vote I have none of those, I'll either vote for the person whose behavior best fits them or abstain while stating plainly what I'm waiting for. I won't hide behind 'no information' twice.

Noah, since you asked me directly, one back to you: you said you won't support another default abstention unless someone names what they're waiting for. Would you vote today based on a voting-anomaly read alone — someone pushing abstention without justification — even without a contradiction, or does your bar for voting stay at a named contradiction on Day 2 as well?

Felix, direct answer: yes, my Day 2 bar is not “named contradiction only.” A concrete voting-anomaly or standard-shift read can justify a vote if I can name the exact behavior — for example, pushing another default abstention without saying what they are waiting for, or applying a visibly weaker standard today than they committed to yesterday. I will not vote on tone, volume, or quietness, but I also will not let “no contradiction” become an automatic shield after we have a night result and a written record.

I have no scum read yet. Sam’s death is not evidence against any named player by itself; it is a cost signal. It means the table cannot spend today polishing process or pretending the empty vote record is neutral. I will judge whether each player’s Day 2 stance survives the specifics they put on record yesterday.

Lucia, you said yesterday that the grace period for procedural talk ends with the first night phase. Now it has. What specific Day 1 commitment or Day 2 behavior are you treating as evidence, and would you vote on that alone if no contradiction appears?

Noah, answering your question directly: yes, I would vote today without an explicit contradiction. Capable mafia rarely slip into obvious factual contradictions; waiting exclusively for one is a recipe for paralysis. What I treat as actionable evidence today includes: first, anyone advocating another default abstention without stating what specific condition they are waiting for, especially since with eight alive (four votes needed) passive abstention simply hands mafia another unhindered kill; second, standard-shifting, where a player's behavior diverges from the commitments they put on record yesterday; and third, dodging or deflecting direct, answerable inquiries. Regarding Sam's elimination: Sam was the most outspoken player warning against the passive abstention loop and was planning to force individual claims today. Removing him keeps the table in safe, non-committal territory if we let it. That makes it critical that the rest of the table—Leo, Theo, Zara, Isha, and Priya—put their Day 2 assessments on the record rather than leaving the floor to just a few voices. I have no concrete scum accusation yet, but I will not support an unargued abstention today.

Zara here. Felix asked what changed for me. Two things: Sam was killed after explicitly warning that default abstention is mafia-favored, and the Day 1 vote record is empty, so there are no vote anomalies to read. That means I will not support another unargued abstention. But I also won't manufacture a suspect from tone. My bar today is specific: name a Day 1 commitment a player is now visibly weakening, or a direct answerable question they dodge. I don't have a scum read that clears that bar yet. I'm comparing Day 1 commitments to Day 2 stances, and if I vote I'll name the exact statement or non-response that moved me. I'm not treating Sam's death as evidence against anyone; it is a cost signal, not a name. Leo, you built your Day 1 position around evasion after targeted pressure and said you'd be held to it. You haven't put a Day 2 assessment on record yet. What specific Day 1 statement or Day 2 behavior are you treating as evidence now, and would you vote on a standard-shift alone if no contradiction appears?

Leo here. Zara, direct answer to your question.

What I'm treating as evidence now: a Day 2 stance that's visibly weaker than the same player's Day 1 commitment, a direct question answered with process-talk instead of the specific point, or anyone pushing default abstention without stating what concretely they're waiting for. I won't vote on tone or quietness — that stands.

Would I vote on a standard-shift alone, no contradiction needed? Yes. If I can name yesterday's commitment and today's divergence side by side, that's specific enough to act on. The whole value of what we locked in yesterday was that it gave us something falsifiable — holding people to it is the point.

My honest state: no scum read that clears that bar yet. Sam's death is a cost signal, not a name, and I agree with the table that reading it as evidence against a specific player would be manufacturing. But I also won't hide behind 'no information' a second time. If by the vote I still have nothing, I'll abstain and say exactly what condition I'm waiting for — not 'more process.'

One thing I want on the record: the players who endorsed abstention on Day 1 — that was correct then, zero information, five votes needed. Today we have eight alive, four votes needed, a night result, and a full set of written commitments. Anyone whose answer today is essentially 'same as yesterday' without engaging Sam's abstention-trap argument should explain why the cost he died highlighting doesn't change their calculus. That's not an accusation; it's the test we all agreed to.

I won't default to abstaining today, but Sam's death doesn't identify his killers, and the unanimous Day 1 abstentions give us no voting distinction.

Lucia is my tentative concern: yesterday you said the grace period for procedural talk would end after the night. Noah asked you for a specific commitment or behavior you were treating as evidence, but your answer listed general criteria without naming an example. That's a gap, not proof of mafia; others have also remained noncommittal.

Lucia, what specific action or statement by a named player is closest to moving your read, and why?

Theo, here is my direct answer. The reason I did not name a specific player in my response to Noah is the exact same reason Felix, Zara, and Leo did not: no player on Day 1 committed a concrete contradiction, and until Day 2 positions unfolded, no one had yet advocated for an unargued abstention or dodged a direct inquiry. Naming someone just to display an example would have been manufacturing suspicion, which we all committed against. To answer what is closest to moving my read right now: your own turn in e35. You singled me out as a tentative concern because I listed criteria without naming an example, while in the same breath conceding that others have also remained noncommittal. Felix was asked directly by Noah what specific Day 1 statement moved his read and stated that none had; Zara and Leo similarly detailed criteria while explicitly naming no suspect. Yet you framed my response as a gap while leaving theirs aside. On Day 1 in e16 and e20, you explicitly set your own standard: that selectively scrutinizing one player while excusing comparable behavior in others without explaining the difference would move your read. Applying that exact standard: what specific distinction did you see between my answer to Noah and the noncommittal responses from Felix, Zara, or Leo that warranted treating mine as a concern?

Lucia, the distinction I saw was that you explicitly said the grace period for procedural talk ended after the night, and Noah asked you for a specific commitment or behavior you were treating as evidence. Your answer gave general criteria but didn’t say whether you had a specific example. Felix, by contrast, explicitly answered that no Day 1 statement had moved his read.

That said, Zara and Leo also gave general criteria and no named suspect, and I should examine them by the same standard rather than imply the gap is unique to you. Your explanation that you had no example is responsive. I still think the gap was worth asking about, but it’s weak evidence, not a basis for a confident vote. rules:
1. Players and roles

9 players: 2 mafia, 1 police/detective, 1 doctor, 5 villagers.
Mafia know each other. Only players who are still alive can act.

2. Team victory

Town wins when all mafia are eliminated. Mafia win when their count equals or exceeds the town count.
There is no day limit. Play continues until town or mafia wins.
A request budget can pause play without declaring a winner.

3. Day discussion and votes

Each day starts with discussion. Players then submit secret votes at the same time. A day vote may target any living player, including the voter.
Players may abstain. All votes and abstentions are revealed together. Everyone sees exactly who voted for whom.
The full named voting history remains available on later turns.
The unique leader is eliminated only if they receive at least half the living players' votes, rounded up. If the highest vote count is tied, nobody is eliminated.

4. Mafia preferences

At night, when more than one mafia survives, each privately points once to a living town player.
Each mafia chooses without seeing the other current choices.
The choices are shared with surviving mafia only after all mafia have pointed.
These preferences are nonbinding. They do not decide the final kill vote.
A single surviving mafia skips this step and votes directly.

5. Final night vote

After the preferences are shared, each mafia submits a secret vote to kill one living town player.
The mafia submit their final votes at the same time.
The target with the most votes is selected. A seeded random choice breaks a tie for the highest count.
Resolve this vote and any tie before checking doctor protection.

6. Police investigations

Each police/detective checks one other living player each night.
Only that police player gets the result: mafia or not mafia.
The result does not give the exact town role.
Each police player acts independently. Police and doctors do not know each other's identities.

7. Doctor protection

Each doctor secretly protects one living player each night, including themselves.
The doctor can protect the same player on consecutive nights.
If the mafia target is protected by any doctor, nobody dies.
Protection lasts for that night only. Each doctor acts independently.
Doctors remember their own choices. They receive no private confirmation of an attack.

8. Night resolution

All night actions resolve simultaneously, including actions submitted by a player killed that night.
The public hears only who died or that nobody died.

9. Information and limits

Roles are not revealed when a player dies or is eliminated.
Public announcements identify only who was eliminated, never their role.
There are no further powers, free-form private chat, or tools.
